title: Customer connectivity acceptance checklist & Terraform iteration log
content:
Purpose:
This is a working doc: an operational acceptance checklist + terraform iteration log for customer VPC/on-prem connectivity handoffs. Intended for SEs + onboarding SREs to run during the first private deployment week. Focus is practical: fast, repeatable checks that catch common failure modes during routing, firewall, and TF module upgrades.

Scope / assumptions:
- Customer provides primary VPC CIDR + peering/transit connectivity (Direct Connect / ExpressRoute / private peering).
- We are responsible for deploying Redwood agents, control plane endpoints (private), and optional egress proxies into customer VPC or connected transit.
- This doc covers L2-L4 connectivity validation, basic L7 smoke tests for API reachability, and a record of Terraform module iterations made during onboarding.
- Not covering deep compliance audit steps (those live in security-and-compliance).

Quick-run sanity checklist (operator):
1) IPs & CIDRs
   - Confirm agreed CIDR ranges for: customer-vpc, redwood-subnet, agent-nics, egress-proxy (record in handoff sheet).
   - Ensure no overlapping /24s with existing customer workloads (common cause of routing blackholes).
2) Routing
   - Verify route tables populated for agent subnets to point to transit/IGW/NAT as required.
   - From a bastion in customer VPC: curl control-plane private endpoint IP: expect 200 with X-Request-Id header.
3) Security groups / NACLs / ACLs
   - Security groups allow agent -> control-plane (TCP 443/HTTPS) and health-check ports (custom: 8081).
   - NACLs are not blocking ephemeral port ranges used by host OS (check 1024-65535 on return traffic).
4) Transit & peering checks
   - BGP session established (if BGP used): check prefixes learned and advertised.
   - Test cross-account routing: ping host in another AZ/region depending on topology.
5) Egress & NAT
   - Confirm NAT gateway or egress proxy is reachable and resolves outbound DNS.
   - Run sample inference call to hosted model to verify outbound TLS handshake and speed (~<200ms baseline).
6) TLS & Certificate validation
   - Control plane cert chain validated from customer hosts; match expected CN/SANs.
7) Metrics & logging
   - Agent logs visible in customer-side log sink (S3/Blob/Fluentd) and include startup sequence.
   - Prometheus / health metrics endpoint reachable from monitoring VPC.
8) Failover test (optional, lower risk window)
   - Simulate transit failover to alternate VPN/Direct connect and verify control-plane fallback within SLA window.

Acceptance test matrix (pass/fail items to record):
- TCP 443 connectivity to control-plane (agent -> cp)
- DNS resolution for control-plane endpoint from both agent hosts and ephemeral test container
- Successful TLS handshake and HTTP 200 to /healthz with expected payload
- KV-cache replication paths (if using multi-region) are visible in metrics
- Inference sample: 10 requests, 95th pct latency below agreed threshold

Terraform iteration log (practical notes):
- Module layout we used: modules/network v0.8.x (local fork during onboarding), modules/egress-proxy, modules/agent-role.
- Key TF variables we changed for customer-A:
   - agent_subnet_count: 2 -> 3 (added small host pool for admin tasks)
   - transit_bgp_asn: replaced placeholder with customer ASN after BGP test
   - enable_strict_nacls: false -> true (note: enabling strict NACLs required updating health-check ports)
- Known TF caveats encountered:
   - aws_ec2_transit_gateway_attachment resource fails with InvalidState if attach attempted while peer TGW is still creating. Workaround: add 3m sleep in apply pipeline or split into two applies (attach-only step).
   - module/network uses account-level default tags; we had to override to ensure tag-based routing policies matched customer naming conventions.
   - Changing VPC CIDR requires full reprovision in our current module layout. For customers likely to adjust ranges, we recommend using smaller, composition-friendly modules (v0.9+ planned refactor).

Upgrade plan (short window approach):
Goal: move from modules/network v0.8 -> v0.9 (safer, non-breaking) within a single low-traffic maintenance window.
- Pre-upgrade (48-72h):
   - Snapshot current TF state and export stateful resources list.
   - Run dry-run plan on staging (mirror customer infra) and collect diffs.
   - Communicate expected downtime (should be none for control-plane but possible short API hiccups).
- Upgrade window (1-2 hours):
   - Lock state, run module upgrades in a staged apply order: networking primitives -> route tables -> transit attachments -> agent groups.
   - Verify each stage via the sanity checklist above.
- Post-upgrade (24h):
   - Monitor metrics for regressions (latency, error-rate). Keep rollback steps at hand.

Rollback plan (if TF apply causes regression):
- If network-level outage: revert to pre-upgrade TF state snapshot and reapply minimal networking apply (attach-only) to restore routes.
- If agent orchestration broke: revert agent module, cordon affected hosts, and redeploy agent pool with previous AMI/config.

Operator tips & gotchas (war stories):
- BGP route flapping was traced to duplicate ASN on customer's firewall appliance; ask for the ASN early and confirm with the network team.
- NACLs are often configured with deny-all rules by default in some customers — validate ephemeral return traffic during discovery calls.
- When migrating TGW attachments across accounts, always confirm the TGW owner ID and apply explicit resource_dependency ordering in TF.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Add a quick-run k8s-side checklist for customers who run agents in EKS/ECS (placeholders in modules/agent-role).
- Add a small module that can compute and suggest non-overlapping CIDR ranges for multi-tenant customers (tech spike).
- Decide on standard retry delays for transit attachment CRs in the apply pipeline (3m vs 5m).

Appendix: quick commands
- Verify BGP: aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-attachments --filters Name=transit-gateway-id,Values=<tgw-id>
- Curl test: curl -v --resolve control.redwood.internal:443:<private-ip> https://control.redwood.internal/healthz
- TF state snapshot: terraform state pull > state-<customer>-2024-08-21.tfstate

Notes to self: keep this doc brief and pragmatic. Ship a small checklist card in the onboarding Kanban; long-form guides live in confluence.

Revision log:
- 2024-08-21 (Maya): initial draft and minimal checklist
- 2024-09-11 (Ben): added TF caveats and attachment sleep workaround
- 2024-11-07 (Aisha): expanded upgrade window steps and rollback notes
